title: Pennsylvania Central Airlines 105
summary: The aircraft approached Runway 18 from the north in a shallow descent that steepened near the approach end. Tower personnel observed it was too high and too fast. title: 1946 Australian National Airways DC-3 crash
summary: Australian National Airways Flight VH-AET departed Hobart on March 10, 1946, with 21 passengers and 3 pilots, one of whom was a supernumerary pilot on his first flights with the airline. The takeoff was normal with both engines operating perfectly. Reaching about 400 ft, the aircraft turned left and descended steeply. It crashed into Frederick Henry Bay less than 2 minutes after takeoff, after flying only 2.9 nautical miles.
probable_cause: The investigation panel concluded the most likely cause was that the automatic pilot was inadvertently engaged shortly after takeoff while the gyroscope was caged. A subsequent inquiry by a Supreme Court judge discovered the captain was diabetic and kept this secret from his employer and the aviation authority, considering this condition probably contributed significantly to the accident.

title: Fairfax, California B-17 Crash
summary: A B-17 Flying Fortress departed Clovis Army Airfield at 4 pm on May 15, carrying pilot Lieutenant Warder Skaggs, three crewmen and 12 passengers bound for Hamilton Army Airfield in Marin County after stops at Davis-Monthan Field and Mines Field near Los Angeles. Around 2 a.m. on May 16, Naval Air Station Oakland radio operators heard the crew reporting they were running low on fuel and lost in fog. Both the crew and Oakland operators mistakenly believed the aircraft was over Oakland Naval Station Airport when it was actually flying over Hamilton Field, nine miles away. Oakland instructed the B-17 to descend to 1500 feet to enable radar pickup. The crew descended but struck the side of White Hill just west of Fairfax, sliding 75 yards down the slope.
probable_cause: Navigation error and fog-induced disorientation led crew and ATC to misidentify the aircraft's position; the crew descended below safe altitude believing they were safe when they were actually over unlit terrain.

Aircraft descended to 1500 feet thinking it was safe but actually descended to terrain height over hills and mountains they could not see due to fog.
Aircraft smashed into the side of White Hill, just west of Fairfax, about nine air miles southwest of Hamilton Field and eighteen miles by road.

title: Mount Tom B-17 crash
summary: A B-17 Flying Fortress transporting soon-to-be-discharged service members from CFB Goose Bay to Mitchel Air Force Base with a stopover at Westover Field departed at 2 p.m. on July 9, 1946. Due to fog and rain, the aircraft circled over Holyoke for almost two hours waiting to land at Westover Field in Chicopee, Massachusetts. The B-17 had been experiencing engine problems with low oil pressure on engine No. 2 which had begun to overheat and smoke. Around 10:20 p.m., the crew made their final approach but due to poor visibility were unable to see the mountain peak on the southern face of Mount Tom. The Civil Aeronautics Authority reported that the fog would have probably prevented the pilot from seeing the beacon light atop Mount Tom. The aircraft slammed into a stone ledge about 200 feet from the summit.
probable_cause: Combination of fog and rain restricting visibility, engine problems on engine No. 2, and crew's descent below the minimum safe altitude without required visual references of the terrain.

title: 1946 C-53 Skytrooper crash on the Gauli Glacier
summary: A C-53 Skytrooper military transport departed Tulln Air Base near Vienna on 18 November 1946 bound for Pisa via Munich, Strasbourg, Dijon and Marseille. The route was chosen to avoid bad weather. Flying in instrument meteorological conditions, the crew became disoriented near Innsbruck. The aircraft encountered a sudden katabatic wind which caused a sudden loss of altitude. The aircraft crashed into the Gauli Glacier at 10,990 feet at 174 mph in deep snow, which rapidly depleted the aircraft's speed. Several people were injured but there were no fatalities. The rescue led to the founding of Swiss air rescue in 1952.

title: 1946 Railway Air Services Dakota crash
summary: Dakota G-AGZA was de-iced and ready to depart Northolt for Glasgow on 19 December 1946 in a snow storm. After an hour-long wait for takeoff clearance, temperature dropped and snow refroze on the wings. When clearance came, the pilot took off with the aircraft almost entirely covered with snow. Unable to gain height due to ice contamination, the aircraft flew a few meters above ground down Angus Drive and struck rooftops of two houses, slewing 90 degrees to rest on the roofs. All 5 occupants and house residents were uninjured, but the aircraft was a total loss.
